{{Short description|Dimensionless astrophysics equation}}
[[Image:LaneEmdenEquation.svg|thumb|Solutions of Lane–Emden equation for ''n'' = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]]

In [[astrophysics]], the '''Lane–Emden equation''' is a dimensionless form of [[Poisson's equation]] for the [[gravitational potential]] of a Newtonian self-gravitating, spherically symmetric, [[polytropic]] fluid. It is named after astrophysicists [[Jonathan Homer Lane]] and [[Robert Emden]].<ref name="Lane1870">{{cite journal|last=Lane|first=Jonathan Homer|author-link=Jonathan Homer Lane|title=On the theoretical temperature of the Sun, under the hypothesis of a gaseous mass maintaining its volume by its internal heat, and depending on the laws of gases as known to terrestrial experiment|journal=American Journal of Science | volume=50| series=2| issue=148| year=1870| pages=57–74| issn=0002-9599| doi=10.2475/ajs.s2-50.148.57| bibcode=1870AmJS...50...57L|s2cid=131102972|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1450030}}</ref> The equation reads
{{Equation box 1|cellpadding|border|indent=:|equation=<math> \frac{1}{\xi^2} \frac{d}{d\xi} \left({\xi^2 \frac{d\theta}{d\xi}}\right) + \theta^n = 0, </math>|border colour=#0073CF|background colour=#F5FFFA}}
where <math>\xi</math> is a dimensionless radius and <math>\theta</math> is related to the density, and thus the pressure, by <math>\rho=\rho_c\theta^n</math> for central density <math>\rho_c</math>. The index <math>n</math> is the polytropic index that appears in the polytropic equation of state,
<math display="block"> P = K \rho^{1 + \frac{1}{n}}\, </math>
where <math>P</math> and <math>\rho</math> are the pressure and density, respectively, and <math>K</math> is a constant of proportionality. The standard boundary conditions are <math>\theta(0)=1</math> and <math>\theta'(0)=0</math>. Solutions thus describe the run of pressure and density with radius and are known as [[polytrope]]s of index <math>n</math>. If an isothermal fluid (polytropic index tends to infinity) is used instead of a polytropic fluid, one obtains the [[Emden–Chandrasekhar equation]].

== Applications ==
Physically, hydrostatic equilibrium connects the gradient of the potential, the density, and the gradient of the pressure, whereas Poisson's equation connects the potential with the density. Thus, if we have a further equation that dictates how the pressure and density vary with respect to one another, we can reach a solution. The particular choice of a polytropic gas as given above makes the mathematical statement of the problem particularly succinct and leads to the Lane–Emden equation. The equation is a useful approximation for self-gravitating spheres of plasma such as stars, but typically it is a rather limiting assumption.

== Derivation ==

=== From hydrostatic equilibrium ===
Consider a self-gravitating, spherically symmetric fluid in [[hydrostatic equilibrium]]. Mass is conserved and thus described by the [[continuity equation]]
<math display="block"> \frac{dm}{dr} = 4\pi r^2 \rho </math>
where <math>\rho</math> is a function of <math>r</math>. The equation of hydrostatic equilibrium is
<math display="block"> \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{dP}{dr} = -\frac{Gm}{r^2} </math>
where <math>m</math> is also a function of <math>r</math>. Differentiating again gives
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dr}\left(\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{dP}{dr}\right) &= \frac{2Gm}{r^3}-\frac{G}{r^2}\frac{dm}{dr} \\
&=-\frac{2}{\rho r}\frac{dP}{dr}-4\pi G\rho
\end{align}</math>
where the continuity equation has been used to replace the mass gradient. Multiplying both sides by <math>r^2</math> and collecting the derivatives of <math>P</math> on the left, one can write
<math display="block"> r^2\frac{d}{dr}\left(\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{dP}{dr}\right)+\frac{2r}{\rho}\frac{dP}{dr}
= \frac{d}{dr}\left(\frac{r^2}{\rho}\frac{dP}{dr}\right)=-4\pi Gr^2\rho </math>

Dividing both sides by <math>r^2</math> yields, in some sense, a dimensional form of the desired equation. If, in addition, we substitute for the polytropic equation of state with <math>P=K\rho_c^{1+\frac{1}{n}}\theta^{n+1}</math> and <math>\rho=\rho_c\theta^n</math>, we have
<math display="block"> \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{d}{dr}\left(r^2K\rho_c^\frac{1}{n}(n+1)\frac{d\theta}{dr}\right)=-4\pi G\rho_c\theta^n</math>

Gathering the constants and substituting <math>r=\alpha\xi</math>, where
<math display="block">\alpha^2=(n+1)K\rho_c^{\frac{1}{n}-1}/4\pi G,</math>
we have the Lane–Emden equation,
<math display="block"> \frac{1}{\xi^2} \frac{d}{d\xi} \left({\xi^2 \frac{d\theta}{d\xi}}\right) + \theta^n = 0 </math>

=== From Poisson's equation ===

Equivalently, one can start with [[Poisson's equation]],
<math display="block"> \nabla^2\Phi=\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{d}{dr}\left( r^2\frac{d\Phi}{dr} \right) = 4\pi G\rho </math>

One can replace the gradient of the potential using the hydrostatic equilibrium, via
<math display="block"> \frac{d\Phi}{dr} = -\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{dP}{dr} </math>
which again yields the dimensional form of the Lane–Emden equation.

==Exact solutions==
For a given value of the polytropic index <math>n</math>, denote the solution to the Lane–Emden equation as <math>\theta_n(\xi)</math>. In general, the Lane–Emden equation must be solved numerically to find <math>\theta_n</math>. There are exact, analytic solutions for certain values of <math>n</math>, in particular: <math>n = 0,1,5</math>.  For <math>n</math> between 0 and 5, the solutions are continuous and finite in extent, with the radius of the star given by <math>R = \alpha \xi_1 </math>, where <math>\theta_n(\xi_1) = 0</math>.

For a given solution <math>\theta_n</math>, the density profile is given by
<math display="block"> \rho = \rho_c \theta_n^n .</math>

The total mass <math>M</math> of the model star can be found by integrating the density over radius, from 0 to <math>\xi_1</math>.

The pressure can be found using the polytropic equation of state, <math>P = K \rho^{1+\frac{1}{n}} </math>, i.e.
<math display="block"> P = K \rho_c^{1+\frac{1}{n}} \theta_n^{n+1}</math>

Finally, if the gas is [[ideal gas law|ideal]], the equation of state is <math>P = k_B\rho T/\mu</math>, where <math>k_B</math> is the [[Boltzmann constant]] and <math>\mu</math> the mean molecular weight. The temperature profile is then given by
<math display="block"> T = \frac{K\mu}{k_B} \rho_c^{1/n} \theta_n </math>

In spherically symmetric cases, the Lane–Emden equation is integrable for only three values of the polytropic index <math>n</math>.

=== For ''n'' = 0 ===
If <math>n = 0</math>, the equation becomes
<math display="block"> \frac{1}{\xi^2} \frac{d}{d\xi} \left( \xi^2 \frac{d\theta}{d\xi} \right) + 1 = 0 </math>

Re-arranging and integrating once gives
<math display="block"> \xi^2\frac{d\theta}{d\xi} = C_1-\frac{1}{3}\xi^3 </math>

Dividing both sides by <math>\xi^2</math> and integrating again gives
<math display="block"> \theta(\xi)=C_0-\frac{C_1}{\xi}-\frac{1}{6}\xi^2 </math>

The boundary conditions <math>\theta(0)=1</math> and <math>\theta'(0)=0</math> imply that the constants of integration are <math>C_0 = 1</math> and <math>C_1 = 0</math>. Therefore,
<math display="block"> \theta(\xi) = 1 - \frac{1}{6}\xi^2</math>

=== For ''n'' = 1 ===
When <math>n = 1</math>, the equation can be expanded in the form
<math display="block"> \frac{d^2\theta}{d\xi^2}+\frac{2}{\xi}\frac{d\theta}{d\xi} + \theta = 0 </math>

One assumes a power series solution:
<math display="block"> \theta(\xi) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n \xi^n </math>

This leads to a recursive relationship for the expansion coefficients:
<math display="block"> a_{n+2} = -\frac{a_n}{(n+3)(n+2)} </math>

This relation can be solved leading to the general solution:
<math display="block"> \theta(\xi)=a_0 \frac{\sin\xi}{\xi} + a_1 \frac{\cos\xi}{\xi} </math>

The [[Boundary value problem|boundary condition]] for a physical polytrope demands that <math> \theta(\xi) \rightarrow 1</math> as <math> \xi \rightarrow 0 </math>.
This requires that <math> a_0 = 1, a_1 = 0 </math>, thus leading to the solution:
<math display="block"> \theta(\xi)=\frac{\sin\xi}{\xi} </math>

=== For ''n'' = 2 ===
This exact solution was found by accident when searching for zero values of the related [[TOV Equation]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pleyer |first1=Jonas |title=Zero Values of the TOV Equation |website=[[GitHub]] |url=https://github.com/jonaspleyer/MasterThesis/ |access-date=4 January 2024}}</ref>

We consider a [[series expansion]] around <math> \theta=0 </math>
<math display="block">
\theta = \sum\limits_{m=0}^\infty a_m \xi^m
</math>
with initial values <math>\theta|_{\xi=0}=\theta_0</math> and <math>\left.\frac{d\theta}{d\xi}\right|_{\xi=0}=0</math>.
Plugging this into the Lane–Emden equation, we can show that all odd coefficients of the series vanish <math>a_{2m+1}=0</math>.
Furthermore, we obtain a recursive relationship between the even coefficients <math>b_m=a_{2m}</math> of the series.
<math display="block">
b_{m+1} = - \frac{1}{(2m+2)(2m+3)}\sum\limits_{k=0}^m b_{m-k}b_k
</math>
The series converges for <math>\xi\lesssim 15.7179</math>.<ref name=":0" />

=== For ''n'' = 5 ===
We start from with the Lane–Emden equation:
<math display="block"> \frac1{\xi^2} {\frac{d}{d\xi}} \left(\xi^2\frac{d\theta}{d\xi}\right) + \theta^5 = 0 </math>

Rewriting for <math> \frac{d\theta}{d\xi} </math> produces:
<math display="block"> \frac{d\theta} {d\xi} = \frac1 2 \left(1+\frac{\xi^2}{3}\right)^{3/2} \frac{2\xi} 3 = \frac {\xi^3}{3 \left[ 1+\frac {\xi^2} 3 \right]^{3/2}}
 </math>

Differentiating with respect to {{mvar|ξ}} leads to:
<math display="block"> \theta^5 =\frac{\xi^2}{\left[1+\frac{\xi^2}{3}\right]^{3/2}} + \frac{3\xi^2}{9\left[1+\frac{\xi^2}3\right]^{5/2}} = \frac 9 {9\left[1+\frac{\xi^2}3\right]^{5/2}}
</math>

Reduced, we come by:
<math display="block">\theta^5 = \frac 1 { \left[ 1+\frac{\xi^2}3 \right]^{5/2}}</math>

Therefore, the Lane–Emden equation has the solution
<math display="block"> \theta(\xi) = \frac 1 {\sqrt{1+\xi^2/3}} </math>
when <math>n = 5</math>. This solution is finite in mass but infinite in radial extent, and therefore the complete polytrope does not represent a physical solution. Chandrasekhar believed for a long time that finding other solution for <math>n=5</math> "is complicated and involves elliptic integrals".

====Srivastava's solution====
In 1962, Sambhunath Srivastava found an explicit solution when <math>n=5</math>.<ref name="Srivastava1962">{{cite journal| last1=Srivastava| first1=Shambhunath| title=A New Solution of the Lane-Emden Equation of Index n=5.|journal=The Astrophysical Journal| volume=136| year=1962| pages=680| issn=0004-637X| doi=10.1086/147421| bibcode=1962ApJ...136..680S}}</ref> His solution is given by
<math display="block">\theta = \frac{\sin(\ln \sqrt \xi)}{\sqrt{3\xi-2\xi \sin^2 (\ln \sqrt\xi)}},</math>
and from this solution, a family of solutions <math>\theta(\xi)\rightarrow \sqrt A\, \theta(A\xi)</math> can be obtained using homology transformation. Since this solution does not satisfy the conditions at the origin (in fact, it is oscillatory with amplitudes growing indefinitely as the origin is approached), this solution can be used in composite stellar models.

== Analytic solutions ==
In applications, the main role play analytic solutions that are expressible by the [[Convergent series|convergent]] [[Power series solution of differential equations|power series]] expanded around some initial point. Typically the expansion point is <math>\xi=0</math>, which is also a singular point (fixed singularity) of the equation, and there is provided some initial data <math>\theta(0)</math> at the centre of the star. One can prove <ref>{{Cite journal| last=Kycia|first=Radosław Antoni| title=Perturbed Lane–Emden Equations as a Boundary Value Problem with Singular Endpoints| journal=Journal of Dynamical and Control Systems| year=2020|language=en|volume=26| issue=2|pages=333–347| doi=10.1007/s10883-019-09445-6| issn=1079-2724|doi-access=free| arxiv=1810.01410}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal| last=Hunter|first=C.| date=2001-12-11| title=Series solutions for polytropes and the isothermal sphere| journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society| language=en| volume=328|issue=3| pages=839–847| doi=10.1046/j.1365-8711.2001.04914.x| bibcode=2001MNRAS.328..839H|issn=0035-8711|doi-access=free}}</ref> that the equation has the convergent power series/analytic solution around the origin of the form
<math display="block">\theta(\xi) = \theta(0) - \frac{\theta(0)^{n}}{6} \xi^{2} + O(\xi^{3}),\quad  \xi \approx 0.</math>

[[File:Lane-Emden n=5 u0=2.gif|alt=Numerical solution of the Lane-Emden equation in the complex plane.|thumb|335x335px|Numerical solution for analytical solution of the Lane-Emden equation in the complex plane for <math>n=5</math>, <math>\theta(0)=2</math>. Two movable singularities on the imaginary axis are visible. They limit the radius of convergence of the analytical solution around the origin. For different values of initial data and <math>p</math> the location of singularities is different, yet they are located symmetrically on the imaginary axis.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Kycia|first1=Radosław Antoni| chapter=On the Singularities of the Emden–Fowler Type Equations|date=2015| chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-319-12577-0_13|title=Current Trends in Analysis and Its Applications | pages=93–99 | editor-last=Mityushev|editor-first=Vladimir V.|place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-12577-0_13 |isbn=978-3-319-12576-3 |access-date=2020-07-19 |last2=Filipuk|first2=Galina |editor2-last=Ruzhansky|editor2-first=Michael V.|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref>]]
The [[radius of convergence]] of this series is limited due to existence <ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal| last1=Kycia| first1=Radosław Antoni| last2=Filipuk| first2=Galina| title=On the generalized Emden–Fowler and isothermal spheres equations| url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0096300315007717| journal=Applied Mathematics and Computation| year=2015| language=en| volume=265| pages=1003–1010| doi=10.1016/j.amc.2015.05.140| url-access=subscription}}</ref> of two singularities on the imaginary axis in the [[complex plane]]. These singularities are located symmetrically with respect to the origin. Their position change when we change equation parameters and the [[initial condition]] <math>\theta(0)</math>, and therefore, they are called [[Painlevé transcendents|movable singularities]] due to classification of the singularities of non-linear ordinary differential equations in the complex plane by [[Paul Painlevé]]. A similar structure of singularities appears in other non-linear equations that result from the reduction of the [[Laplace operator]] in spherical symmetry, e.g., Isothermal Sphere equation.<ref name=":1" />

Analytic solutions can be extended along the [[Number line|real line]] by [[analytic continuation]] procedure resulting in the full profile of the star or [[molecular cloud]] cores. Two analytic solutions with the overlapping [[circle of convergence|circles of convergence]] can also be matched on the overlap to the larger domain solution, which is a commonly used method of construction of profiles of required properties.

The series solution is also used in the [[numerical integration]] of the equation. It is used to shift the initial data for analytic solution slightly away from the origin since at the origin the numerical methods fail due to the singularity of the equation.

== Numerical solutions ==
In general, solutions are found by numerical integration. Many standard methods require that the problem is formulated as a system of first-order [[ordinary differential equation]]s. For example,<ref>{{cite book |last1= Hansen |first1= Carl J. |last2= Kawaler |first2= Steven D. |last3= Trimble |first3= Virginia |date= 2004|title= Stellar Interiors: Physical Principles, Structure, and Evolution |location= New York, NY |publisher= Springer |page= 338 |isbn= 9780387200897}}</ref>
:<math>
\begin{align}
& \frac{d\theta}{d\xi}=-\frac{\varphi}{\xi^2} \\[6pt]
& \frac{d\varphi}{d\xi}=\theta^n\xi^2
\end{align}
</math>

Here, <math>\varphi(\xi)</math> is interpreted as the dimensionless mass, defined by <math>m(r) = 4\pi\alpha^3\rho_c\varphi(\xi)</math>. The relevant initial conditions are <math>\varphi(0) = 0</math> and <math>\theta(0) = 1</math>. The first equation represents hydrostatic equilibrium and the second represents mass conservation.

== Homologous variables ==

=== Homology-invariant equation ===
It is known that if <math>\theta(\xi)</math> is a solution of the Lane–Emden equation, then so is <math>C^{2/n+1}\theta(C\xi)</math>.<ref name="Chandrasekhar1957">{{cite book|last=Chandrasekhar|first=Subrahmanyan |title=An Introduction to the Study of Stellar Structure| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VwPLAgAAQBAJ|year=1957|publisher=Dover|isbn=978-0-486-60413-8|bibcode=1939isss.book.....C|author-link=Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar|orig-year=1939}}</ref> Solutions that are related in this way are called ''homologous''; the process that transforms them is ''homology''. If one chooses variables that are invariant to homology, then we can reduce the order of the Lane–Emden equation by one.

A variety of such variables exist. A suitable choice is
<math display="block">U=\frac{d\log m}{d\log r}=\frac{\xi^3\theta^n} \varphi </math>
and
<math display="block">V = \frac{d\log P}{d\log r}=(n+1)\frac \varphi {\xi\theta}</math>

We can differentiate the logarithms of these variables with respect to <math>\xi</math>, which gives
<math display="block">\frac{1}{U} \frac{dU}{d\xi} = \frac 1 \xi \left(3 - n(n+1)^{-1}V - U \right)</math>
and
<math display="block">\frac{1}{V} \frac{dV}{d\xi} = \frac 1 \xi \left(-1 + U + (n+1)^{-1}V \right).</math>

Finally, we can divide these two equations to eliminate the dependence on <math>\xi</math>, which leaves
<math display="block">\frac{dV}{dU} = -\frac{V}{U}\left(\frac{U+(n+1)^{-1}V-1}{U+n(n+1)^{-1}V-3}\right).</math>

This is now a single first-order equation.

=== Topology of the homology-invariant equation ===

The homology-invariant equation can be regarded as the autonomous pair of equations
<math display="block">\frac{dU}{d\log\xi} = -U \left(U+n(n+1)^{-1}V-3\right)</math>
and
<math display="block">\frac{dV}{d\log\xi} = V \left(U+(n+1)^{-1}V-1\right).</math>

The behaviour of solutions to these equations can be determined by [[linear stability]] analysis. The critical points of the equation (where <math>dV/d\log\xi = dU/d\log\xi = 0</math>) and the [[eigenvalues and eigenvectors]] of the [[Jacobian matrix]] are tabulated below.<ref name="Horedt1987">{{cite journal|last=Horedt|first=Georg P.|title=Topology of the Lane-Emden equation|journal=[[Astronomy and Astrophysics]] | date=1987 | volume=117|issue=1–2|pages=117–130|bibcode=1987A&A...177..117H|issn=0004-6361}}</ref>
{| class="wikitable"
! Critical point !! Eigenvalues !! Eigenvectors
|-
| <math>(0,0)</math> || <math>3, -1</math> || <math>(1,0), (0,1)</math>
|-
| <math>(3,0)</math> || <math>-3,2</math> || <math>(1,0), (-3n,5+5n)</math>
|-
| <math>(0,n+1)</math> || <math>1, 3-n</math> || <math>(0,1), (2-n,1+n)</math>
|-
| <math>\left(\dfrac{n-3}{n-1},2\dfrac{n+1}{n-1}\right)</math> || <math>\dfrac{n-5\pm\Delta_n}{2-2n}</math> || <math>(1-n\mp\Delta_n,4+4n)</math>
|}
